[Medium] read-only-rootfs
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Deployment/emptydir-no-limit
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" does not have a read-only root filesystem.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

A writable root filesystem allows an attacker who gains code execution in your container to modify application binaries, install attack tools, plant backdoors, or persist malware across container restarts. Making the filesystem read-only eliminates an entire class of post-exploitation techniques.

## How to Fix

Enable a read-only root filesystem and mount writable volumes only where needed:

```yaml
securityContext:
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
volumeMounts:
  - name: tmp
    mountPath: /tmp
volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}
```

Common paths that need write access include /tmp, /var/cache, and /var/run. Mount each as an emptyDir or tmpfs volume rather than making the entire filesystem writable.

## Learn More

This aligns with CIS Benchmark 5.2.4 and the defense-in-depth principle. Combined with dropping capabilities and running as non-root, a read-only filesystem forms a strong container hardening baseline.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1565.001 · NSA 1.2

[Medium] resource-limits-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Deployment/emptydir-no-limit
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" is missing both CPU and memory limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without resource limits, a single container can consume all available CPU and memory on a node, starving other workloads and triggering cascading failures. An attacker who compromises an unlimited container can mount a denial-of-service attack against the entire node with a simple fork bomb or memory allocation loop.

## How to Fix

Set both CPU and memory limits based on your application's actual resource usage:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 256Mi
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
```

Profile your application under load to determine appropriate values. Set limits to handle peak usage and requests to match steady-state consumption.

## Learn More

Use LimitRange objects to enforce default limits at the namespace level. Resource limits also determine the pod's QoS class: pods with equal requests and limits get Guaranteed QoS and are last to be evicted.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Medium] resource-requests-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Deployment/emptydir-no-limit
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" is missing both CPU and memory requests.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Resource requests tell the Kubernetes scheduler how much CPU and memory your container needs. Without requests, the scheduler treats the pod as needing zero resources and may pack too many pods onto a single node. This leads to overcommitment, resource contention, throttling, and OOM kills under load.

## How to Fix

Set resource requests based on your application's steady-state usage:

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 256Mi
```

Observe your application's actual resource consumption using `kubectl top` or a monitoring tool, then set requests to match the typical steady-state usage.

## Learn More

Resource requests determine the pod's QoS class and scheduling behavior. Pods with requests equal to limits receive Guaranteed QoS. Use Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) to automatically recommend request values.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.requests
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Medium] token-projection-config
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Deployment/emptydir-no-limit
  Message:     Deployment "emptydir-no-limit" does not use explicitly configured projected ServiceAccount tokens with expiry and audience restrictions.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without explicit projection configuration, ServiceAccount tokens use Kubernetes defaults: no audience restriction and a long expiration. A stolen token remains valid for an extended period and can be used against any API server endpoint, widening the blast radius of a compromise.

## How to Fix

Add a projected volume with explicit expiration and audience:

```yaml
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: token
      projected:
        sources:
          - serviceAccountToken:
              expirationSeconds: 3600
              audience: my-api
              path: token
  containers:
    - name: app
      volumeMounts:
        - name: token
          mountPath: /var/run/secrets/tokens
          readOnly: true
```

Projected tokens auto-rotate before expiry and are rejected by endpoints outside the specified audience.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on projected volumes and service account token volume projection for detailed configuration options.
  Field:       .spec.volumes
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.1.6 · MITRE T1552.007 · NSA 3.2

Each cloud provider has its own encryption parameter: AWS EBS (`encrypted: "true"`), GCP PD (CMEK via `disk-encryption-kms-key`), Azure Disk (SSE enabled by default).

## Learn More

See your cloud provider's CSI driver documentation for encryption configuration. The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark recommends encrypting persistent volumes at rest.
  Field:       .spec.storageClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.4.2 · MITRE T1530 · NSA 5.2

[Medium] network-policy-egress-unrestricted
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Namespace/kv-e2e-storage
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-storage" has no NetworkPolicy with egress restrictions. Pods can reach any external destination.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without any egress NetworkPolicy in this namespace, pods can freely send traffic to any destination including the public internet. A compromised pod can exfiltrate sensitive data, reach cloud metadata services (e.g., 169.254.169.254), or establish reverse shells to attacker-controlled servers.

## How to Fix

Create a NetworkPolicy with `Egress` in `policyTypes` to restrict outbound traffic. At minimum, allow DNS resolution:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-egress
  namespace: my-namespace
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector: {}
      ports:
        - port: 53
          protocol: UDP
```

Add additional egress rules for specific services your workloads need to reach.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes NetworkPolicy documentation and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.3.2. Egress controls are a key defense-in-depth measure recommended by the NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guide.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.3.2 · MITRE T1048 · NSA 4.2

[Medium] psa-labels-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Namespace/kv-e2e-storage
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-storage" is missing the pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce label; pod security is not enforced.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without PSA enforcement labels, any pod configuration is allowed in this namespace, including privileged containers, host namespace access, and root execution. This bypasses Kubernetes' built-in Pod Security Standards and leaves the namespace vulnerable to workloads that could compromise the node.

## How to Fix

Add Pod Security Admission labels to enforce a security profile on all pods in the namespace:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: kv-e2e-storage
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
```

Start with `baseline` enforcement to block known privilege escalations, then upgrade to `restricted` after verifying all workloads are compliant.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Security Admission documentation and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2. The three-tier approach (enforce, audit, warn) allows gradual adoption of stricter profiles.
  Field:       .metadata.labels
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.1 · MITRE T1610 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] apparmor-profile
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" does not have an AppArmor profile set.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

AppArmor provides mandatory access control (MAC) that restricts which files, network resources, and capabilities a container process can access. Without an AppArmor profile, the container operates without these restrictions, allowing an attacker with code execution to access any file the container user can read and make unrestricted network connections.

## How to Fix

Apply an AppArmor profile in the container's securityContext (Kubernetes 1.30+):

```yaml
securityContext:
  appArmorProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
```

The RuntimeDefault profile provides sensible restrictions for most applications. For tighter control, create a custom Localhost profile that only allows the specific file and network access your application needs.

## Learn More

AppArmor is available on Debian/Ubuntu-based nodes. RHEL/CentOS nodes use SELinux instead. Both provide MAC enforcement. Refer to CIS Benchmark 5.7.5 and the Kubernetes AppArmor documentation.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.appArmorProfile
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] capabilities-not-dropped
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" does not drop ALL capabilities, leaving it with unnecessary default privileges.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

By default, containers receive a set of Linux capabilities including KILL, SETUID, SETGID, and NET_RAW. These defaults are rarely needed by application code and significantly increase the potential damage from a container compromise. Dropping all capabilities follows the principle of least privilege.

## How to Fix

Explicitly drop all capabilities and selectively add back only what your application needs:

```yaml
securityContext:
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"]
    add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]  # Only if needed
```

Most web applications, API servers, and background workers run perfectly with all capabilities dropped. Test your application after making this change to confirm no functionality is lost.

## Learn More

This is required by the Pod Security Standards "Restricted" profile and aligns with CIS Benchmark 5.2.7. Kubernetes best practice is to treat capability grants as exceptions that require explicit justification.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.capabilities.drop
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.8 · CIS 5.2.10 · MITRE T1068 · NSA 1.1

[Medium] image-pull-policy
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" uses a mutable image tag with pullPolicy "IfNotPresent" (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), risking stale images.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

When a mutable image tag is used without `imagePullPolicy: Always`, Kubernetes may serve a cached version of the image from the node. If the tag has been updated in the registry (with a security patch or -- worse -- a compromised layer), the running container will not reflect those changes.

## How to Fix

Set `imagePullPolicy: Always` for any container using a mutable tag:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:1.25.3
    imagePullPolicy: Always   # Forces fresh pull each time
```

Alternatively, pin images by digest (`image@sha256:...`), which makes the pull policy irrelevant because the content is immutable.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on image pull policies and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.4.2 for pull policy guidance.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].imagePullPolicy
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Medium] projected-volume-security
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Message:     Pod "projected-permissive" has projected volume "sa-token" with defaultMode 0644 which is too permissive.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Projected volumes with overly permissive file modes allow any process in the pod to read sensitive data such as service account tokens and secrets. If a container is compromised, the attacker can easily harvest these credentials to escalate privileges or move laterally within the cluster.

## How to Fix

Reduce the defaultMode to restrict file access:

```yaml
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: sa-token
      projected:
        defaultMode: 0400         # Owner read-only (was too permissive)
        sources:
          - serviceAccountToken:
              path: token
```

Use 0400 for read-only access or 0600 if the application must write to the mounted files.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Projected Volumes documentation for defaultMode details. The CIS Benchmark recommends file modes of 0600 or lower for sensitive volume mounts to limit exposure within the pod.
  Field:       .spec.volumes[0].projected.defaultMode
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.4.1 · MITRE T1552 · NSA 5.1

[Medium] psa-restricted-violations
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Pod "projected-permissive" container "pause" violates PSS Restricted: runAsNonRoot is not true.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Running as root inside a container means that any container escape vulnerability immediately grants root access on the host node. Even without an escape, root inside the container can modify sensitive files, install packages, and access capabilities that non-root users cannot.

## How to Fix

Set `runAsNonRoot: true` and specify a non-root user ID in the security context:

```yaml
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000
  runAsGroup: 1000
```

Set this at the pod level to apply to all containers. Ensure your container image supports running as a non-root user (many official images do).

## Learn More

See the Pod Security Standards Restricted profile and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.6. Running as non-root is a fundamental container security best practice.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.runAsNonRoot
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.1 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] psa-restricted-violations
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Pod "projected-permissive" container "pause" violates PSS Restricted: allowPrivilegeEscalation is not false.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

When `allowPrivilegeEscalation` is true (the default), processes inside the container can gain more privileges than their parent process. This enables attacks via setuid/setgid binaries, kernel exploits, and other escalation vectors that can lead to container escape.

## How to Fix

Explicitly set `allowPrivilegeEscalation` to false in the container's security context:

```yaml
securityContext:
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  runAsNonRoot: true
  capabilities:
    drop: [ALL]
```

This prevents setuid binaries and other privilege escalation vectors from working inside the container.

## Learn More

See the Pod Security Standards Restricted profile and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.5. Disabling privilege escalation is required for PSS Restricted compliance.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.1 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] psa-restricted-violations
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Pod "projected-permissive" container "pause" violates PSS Restricted: capabilities.drop does not include ALL.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

By default, containers receive a set of Linux capabilities that may be exploited for privilege escalation. Without explicitly dropping ALL capabilities, containers retain permissions like NET_RAW (enabling packet spoofing) and FOWNER (bypassing file permission checks).

## How to Fix

Drop all capabilities and add back only the specific ones your application requires:

```yaml
securityContext:
  capabilities:
    drop: [ALL]
    add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]  # Only if binding to ports below 1024
```

Most applications work correctly with all capabilities dropped. Test your workload first and add back only capabilities that cause failures.

## Learn More

See the Pod Security Standards Restricted profile and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.7. Dropping ALL capabilities is required for PSS Restricted compliance.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.capabilities.drop
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.1 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] read-only-rootfs
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" does not have a read-only root filesystem.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

A writable root filesystem allows an attacker who gains code execution in your container to modify application binaries, install attack tools, plant backdoors, or persist malware across container restarts. Making the filesystem read-only eliminates an entire class of post-exploitation techniques.

## How to Fix

Enable a read-only root filesystem and mount writable volumes only where needed:

```yaml
securityContext:
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
volumeMounts:
  - name: tmp
    mountPath: /tmp
volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}
```

Common paths that need write access include /tmp, /var/cache, and /var/run. Mount each as an emptyDir or tmpfs volume rather than making the entire filesystem writable.

## Learn More

This aligns with CIS Benchmark 5.2.4 and the defense-in-depth principle. Combined with dropping capabilities and running as non-root, a read-only filesystem forms a strong container hardening baseline.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1565.001 · NSA 1.2

[Medium] resource-limits-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" is missing both CPU and memory limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without resource limits, a single container can consume all available CPU and memory on a node, starving other workloads and triggering cascading failures. An attacker who compromises an unlimited container can mount a denial-of-service attack against the entire node with a simple fork bomb or memory allocation loop.

## How to Fix

Set both CPU and memory limits based on your application's actual resource usage:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 256Mi
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
```

Profile your application under load to determine appropriate values. Set limits to handle peak usage and requests to match steady-state consumption.

## Learn More

Use LimitRange objects to enforce default limits at the namespace level. Resource limits also determine the pod's QoS class: pods with equal requests and limits get Guaranteed QoS and are last to be evicted.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Medium] resource-requests-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" is missing both CPU and memory requests.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Resource requests tell the Kubernetes scheduler how much CPU and memory your container needs. Without requests, the scheduler treats the pod as needing zero resources and may pack too many pods onto a single node. This leads to overcommitment, resource contention, throttling, and OOM kills under load.

## How to Fix

Set resource requests based on your application's steady-state usage:

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 256Mi
```

Observe your application's actual resource consumption using `kubectl top` or a monitoring tool, then set requests to match the typical steady-state usage.

## Learn More

Resource requests determine the pod's QoS class and scheduling behavior. Pods with requests equal to limits receive Guaranteed QoS. Use Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) to automatically recommend request values.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.requests
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Medium] run-as-group
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" does not set runAsGroup; the process will run as GID 0 (root group) by default.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without an explicit runAsGroup, the container process defaults to GID 0 (the root group). Files and sockets owned by the root group become accessible to the container, including potentially sensitive host files if volumes are mounted. This widens the attack surface unnecessarily.

## How to Fix

Set an explicit non-root group in the securityContext:

```yaml
securityContext:
  runAsGroup: 1000
  runAsUser: 1000
  runAsNonRoot: true
```

Ensure the container image's application files and directories are readable by the specified GID. You may need to adjust file ownership in your Dockerfile with `chown`.

## Learn More

This aligns with CIS Benchmark 5.2.6 and the Pod Security Standards "Restricted" profile. Always set runAsUser, runAsGroup, and runAsNonRoot together for comprehensive identity control.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.runAsGroup
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.7 · MITRE T1068 · NSA 1.1

[Medium] seccomp-profile
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" does not have a Seccomp profile set at either the container or pod level.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a Seccomp profile, containers can invoke any of the 300+ Linux system calls, leaving the entire kernel attack surface exposed. Kernel vulnerabilities in obscure syscalls are a primary vector for container escapes. Seccomp filtering blocks dangerous syscalls that legitimate applications never use.

## How to Fix

Apply a Seccomp profile at the container or pod level:

```yaml
securityContext:
  seccompProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
```

The RuntimeDefault profile blocks approximately 50 dangerous syscalls while allowing normal application behavior. For stricter controls, use a custom Localhost profile tailored to your application's needs. Set the profile at the pod level to apply it to all containers.

## Learn More

Seccomp profiles are required by the Pod Security Standards "Restricted" profile and CIS Benchmark 5.7.2. Use tools like `strace` or the Security Profiles Operator to generate custom profiles for your workloads.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.seccompProfile
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.2 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] pvc-no-encryption
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/PersistentVolumeClaim/shared-data-rwx
  Message:     PVC "shared-data-rwx" uses StorageClass "kv-e2e-nfs-unencrypted" which has no encryption configuration.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

PVCs without encryption store data in plaintext on the underlying disk. If the storage media is decommissioned, stolen, or accessed by an unauthorized party, all data is readable. This is especially critical for volumes storing credentials, PII, or financial data.

## How to Fix

Create a StorageClass with encryption enabled and reference it in your PVC:

```yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: encrypted-gp3
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
parameters:
  encrypted: "true"
  kmsKeyId: arn:aws:kms:...:key/...   # Optional: customer-managed key
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
spec:
  storageClassName: encrypted-gp3
```

Each cloud provider has its own encryption parameter: AWS EBS (`encrypted: "true"`), GCP PD (CMEK via `disk-encryption-kms-key`), Azure Disk (SSE enabled by default).

## Learn More

See your cloud provider's CSI driver documentation for encryption configuration. The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark recommends encrypting persistent volumes at rest.
  Field:       .spec.storageClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.4.2 · MITRE T1530 · NSA 5.2

Set `imagePullPolicy: Always` for any container using a mutable tag:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:1.25.3
    imagePullPolicy: Always   # Forces fresh pull each time
```

Alternatively, pin images by digest (`image@sha256:...`), which makes the pull policy irrelevant because the content is immutable.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on image pull policies and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.4.2 for pull policy guidance.
  Field:       .spec.containers[1].imagePullPolicy
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Medium] psa-restricted-violations
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/dangerous-capabilities
  Container:   caps-sys-admin
  Message:     Deployment "dangerous-capabilities" container "caps-sys-admin" violates PSS Restricted: runAsNonRoot is not true.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Running as root inside a container means that any container escape vulnerability immediately grants root access on the host node. Even without an escape, root inside the container can modify sensitive files, install packages, and access capabilities that non-root users cannot.

## How to Fix

Set `runAsNonRoot: true` and specify a non-root user ID in the security context:

```yaml
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000
  runAsGroup: 1000
```

Set this at the pod level to apply to all containers. Ensure your container image supports running as a non-root user (many official images do).

## Learn More

See the Pod Security Standards Restricted profile and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.6. Running as non-root is a fundamental container security best practice.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.runAsNonRoot
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.1 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] psa-restricted-violations
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/dangerous-capabilities
  Container:   caps-sys-admin
  Message:     Deployment "dangerous-capabilities" container "caps-sys-admin" violates PSS Restricted: allowPrivilegeEscalation is not false.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

When `allowPrivilegeEscalation` is true (the default), processes inside the container can gain more privileges than their parent process. This enables attacks via setuid/setgid binaries, kernel exploits, and other escalation vectors that can lead to container escape.

## How to Fix

Explicitly set `allowPrivilegeEscalation` to false in the container's security context:

```yaml
securityContext:
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  runAsNonRoot: true
  capabilities:
    drop: [ALL]
```

This prevents setuid binaries and other privilege escalation vectors from working inside the container.

## Learn More

See the Pod Security Standards Restricted profile and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.5. Disabling privilege escalation is required for PSS Restricted compliance.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.1 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] psa-restricted-violations
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/dangerous-capabilities
  Container:   caps-sys-admin
  Message:     Deployment "dangerous-capabilities" container "caps-sys-admin" violates PSS Restricted: capabilities.drop does not include ALL.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

By default, containers receive a set of Linux capabilities that may be exploited for privilege escalation. Without explicitly dropping ALL capabilities, containers retain permissions like NET_RAW (enabling packet spoofing) and FOWNER (bypassing file permission checks).

## How to Fix

Drop all capabilities and add back only the specific ones your application requires:

```yaml
securityContext:
  capabilities:
    drop: [ALL]
    add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]  # Only if binding to ports below 1024
```

Most applications work correctly with all capabilities dropped. Test your workload first and add back only capabilities that cause failures.

## Learn More

See the Pod Security Standards Restricted profile and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.7. Dropping ALL capabilities is required for PSS Restricted compliance.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.capabilities.drop
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.1 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] read-only-rootfs
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/dangerous-capabilities
  Container:   caps-sys-admin
  Message:     Container "caps-sys-admin" does not have a read-only root filesystem.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

A writable root filesystem allows an attacker who gains code execution in your container to modify application binaries, install attack tools, plant backdoors, or persist malware across container restarts. Making the filesystem read-only eliminates an entire class of post-exploitation techniques.

## How to Fix

Enable a read-only root filesystem and mount writable volumes only where needed:

```yaml
securityContext:
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
volumeMounts:
  - name: tmp
    mountPath: /tmp
volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}
```

Common paths that need write access include /tmp, /var/cache, and /var/run. Mount each as an emptyDir or tmpfs volume rather than making the entire filesystem writable.

## Learn More

This aligns with CIS Benchmark 5.2.4 and the defense-in-depth principle. Combined with dropping capabilities and running as non-root, a read-only filesystem forms a strong container hardening baseline.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1565.001 · NSA 1.2

[Medium] read-only-rootfs
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/dangerous-capabilities

[Medium] resource-limits-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/dangerous-capabilities
  Container:   caps-sys-admin
  Message:     Container "caps-sys-admin" is missing both CPU and memory limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without resource limits, a single container can consume all available CPU and memory on a node, starving other workloads and triggering cascading failures. An attacker who compromises an unlimited container can mount a denial-of-service attack against the entire node with a simple fork bomb or memory allocation loop.

## How to Fix

Set both CPU and memory limits based on your application's actual resource usage:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 256Mi
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
```

Profile your application under load to determine appropriate values. Set limits to handle peak usage and requests to match steady-state consumption.

## Learn More

Use LimitRange objects to enforce default limits at the namespace level. Resource limits also determine the pod's QoS class: pods with equal requests and limits get Guaranteed QoS and are last to be evicted.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Medium] resource-requests-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/dangerous-capabilities
  Container:   caps-sys-admin
  Message:     Container "caps-sys-admin" is missing both CPU and memory requests.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Resource requests tell the Kubernetes scheduler how much CPU and memory your container needs. Without requests, the scheduler treats the pod as needing zero resources and may pack too many pods onto a single node. This leads to overcommitment, resource contention, throttling, and OOM kills under load.

## How to Fix

Set resource requests based on your application's steady-state usage:

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 256Mi
```

Observe your application's actual resource consumption using `kubectl top` or a monitoring tool, then set requests to match the typical steady-state usage.

## Learn More

Resource requests determine the pod's QoS class and scheduling behavior. Pods with requests equal to limits receive Guaranteed QoS. Use Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) to automatically recommend request values.

[Medium] run-as-group
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/dangerous-capabilities
  Container:   caps-sys-admin
  Message:     Container "caps-sys-admin" does not set runAsGroup; the process will run as GID 0 (root group) by default.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

## How to Fix

```yaml
securityContext:
  runAsGroup: 1000
  runAsUser: 1000
  runAsNonRoot: true
```

Ensure the container image's application files and directories are readable by the specified GID. You may need to adjust file ownership in your Dockerfile with `chown`.

## Learn More

This aligns with CIS Benchmark 5.2.6 and the Pod Security Standards "Restricted" profile. Always set runAsUser, runAsGroup, and runAsNonRoot together for comprehensive identity control.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.runAsGroup

[Medium] seccomp-profile
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/dangerous-capabilities
  Container:   caps-sys-admin
  Message:     Container "caps-sys-admin" does not have a Seccomp profile set at either the container or pod level.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a Seccomp profile, containers can invoke any of the 300+ Linux system calls, leaving the entire kernel attack surface exposed. Kernel vulnerabilities in obscure syscalls are a primary vector for container escapes. Seccomp filtering blocks dangerous syscalls that legitimate applications never use.

## How to Fix

Apply a Seccomp profile at the container or pod level:

```yaml
securityContext:
  seccompProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
```

The RuntimeDefault profile blocks approximately 50 dangerous syscalls while allowing normal application behavior. For stricter controls, use a custom Localhost profile tailored to your application's needs. Set the profile at the pod level to apply it to all containers.

## Learn More

Seccomp profiles are required by the Pod Security Standards "Restricted" profile and CIS Benchmark 5.7.2. Use tools like `strace` or the Security Profiles Operator to generate custom profiles for your workloads.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.seccompProfile
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.2 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] seccomp-profile
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/dangerous-capabilities

  Message:     Container "caps-not-dropped" does not have a Seccomp profile set at either the container or pod level.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a Seccomp profile, containers can invoke any of the 300+ Linux system calls, leaving the entire kernel attack surface exposed. Kernel vulnerabilities in obscure syscalls are a primary vector for container escapes. Seccomp filtering blocks dangerous syscalls that legitimate applications never use.

## How to Fix

Apply a Seccomp profile at the container or pod level:

```yaml
securityContext:
  seccompProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
```

The RuntimeDefault profile blocks approximately 50 dangerous syscalls while allowing normal application behavior. For stricter controls, use a custom Localhost profile tailored to your application's needs. Set the profile at the pod level to apply it to all containers.

## Learn More

Seccomp profiles are required by the Pod Security Standards "Restricted" profile and CIS Benchmark 5.7.2. Use tools like `strace` or the Security Profiles Operator to generate custom profiles for your workloads.
  Field:       .spec.containers[2].securityContext.seccompProfile
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.2 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] token-projection-config
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/dangerous-capabilities
  Message:     Deployment "dangerous-capabilities" does not use explicitly configured projected ServiceAccount tokens with expiry and audience restrictions.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without explicit projection configuration, ServiceAccount tokens use Kubernetes defaults: no audience restriction and a long expiration. A stolen token remains valid for an extended period and can be used against any API server endpoint, widening the blast radius of a compromise.

## How to Fix

Add a projected volume with explicit expiration and audience:

```yaml
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: token
      projected:
        sources:
          - serviceAccountToken:
              expirationSeconds: 3600
              audience: my-api
              path: token
  containers:
    - name: app
      volumeMounts:
        - name: token
          mountPath: /var/run/secrets/tokens
          readOnly: true
```

Projected tokens auto-rotate before expiry and are rejected by endpoints outside the specified audience.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on projected volumes and service account token volume projection for detailed configuration options.
  Field:       .spec.volumes
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.1.6 · MITRE T1552.007 · NSA 3.2

[Medium] apparmor-profile
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/default-sa-automount
  Container:   app
  Message:     Container "app" does not have an AppArmor profile set.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

AppArmor provides mandatory access control (MAC) that restricts which files, network resources, and capabilities a container process can access. Without an AppArmor profile, the container operates without these restrictions, allowing an attacker with code execution to access any file the container user can read and make unrestricted network connections.

## How to Fix

Apply an AppArmor profile in the container's securityContext (Kubernetes 1.30+):

```yaml
securityContext:
  appArmorProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
```

The RuntimeDefault profile provides sensible restrictions for most applications. For tighter control, create a custom Localhost profile that only allows the specific file and network access your application needs.

## Learn More

AppArmor is available on Debian/Ubuntu-based nodes. RHEL/CentOS nodes use SELinux instead. Both provide MAC enforcement. Refer to CIS Benchmark 5.7.5 and the Kubernetes AppArmor documentation.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.appArmorProfile
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] capabilities-not-dropped
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/default-sa-automount
  Container:   app
  Message:     Container "app" does not drop ALL capabilities, leaving it with unnecessary default privileges.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

By default, containers receive a set of Linux capabilities including KILL, SETUID, SETGID, and NET_RAW. These defaults are rarely needed by application code and significantly increase the potential damage from a container compromise. Dropping all capabilities follows the principle of least privilege.

## How to Fix

Explicitly drop all capabilities and selectively add back only what your application needs:

```yaml
securityContext:
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"]
    add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]  # Only if needed
```

Most web applications, API servers, and background workers run perfectly with all capabilities dropped. Test your application after making this change to confirm no functionality is lost.

## Learn More

This is required by the Pod Security Standards "Restricted" profile and aligns with CIS Benchmark 5.2.7. Kubernetes best practice is to treat capability grants as exceptions that require explicit justification.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.capabilities.drop
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.8 · CIS 5.2.10 · MITRE T1068 · NSA 1.1

[Medium] image-pull-policy
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/default-sa-automount
  Container:   app
  Message:     Container "app" uses a mutable image tag with pullPolicy "IfNotPresent" (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), risking stale images.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

When a mutable image tag is used without `imagePullPolicy: Always`, Kubernetes may serve a cached version of the image from the node. If the tag has been updated in the registry (with a security patch or -- worse -- a compromised layer), the running container will not reflect those changes.

## How to Fix

Set `imagePullPolicy: Always` for any container using a mutable tag:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:1.25.3
    imagePullPolicy: Always   # Forces fresh pull each time
```

Alternatively, pin images by digest (`image@sha256:...`), which makes the pull policy irrelevant because the content is immutable.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on image pull policies and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.4.2 for pull policy guidance.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].imagePullPolicy
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Medium] projected-volume-security
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/default-sa-automount
  Message:     Pod "default-sa-automount" has projected volume "kube-api-access-z5rjm" with defaultMode 0644 which is too permissive.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Projected volumes with overly permissive file modes allow any process in the pod to read sensitive data such as service account tokens and secrets. If a container is compromised, the attacker can easily harvest these credentials to escalate privileges or move laterally within the cluster.

## How to Fix

Reduce the defaultMode to restrict file access:

```yaml
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: kube-api-access-z5rjm
      projected:
        defaultMode: 0400         # Owner read-only (was too permissive)
        sources:
          - serviceAccountToken:
              path: token
```

Use 0400 for read-only access or 0600 if the application must write to the mounted files.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Projected Volumes documentation for defaultMode details. The CIS Benchmark recommends file modes of 0600 or lower for sensitive volume mounts to limit exposure within the pod.
  Field:       .spec.volumes[0].projected.defaultMode
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.4.1 · MITRE T1552 · NSA 5.1

[Medium] psa-restricted-violations
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/default-sa-automount
  Container:   app
  Message:     Pod "default-sa-automount" container "app" violates PSS Restricted: runAsNonRoot is not true.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Running as root inside a container means that any container escape vulnerability immediately grants root access on the host node. Even without an escape, root inside the container can modify sensitive files, install packages, and access capabilities that non-root users cannot.

## How to Fix

Set `runAsNonRoot: true` and specify a non-root user ID in the security context:

```yaml
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000
  runAsGroup: 1000
```

Set this at the pod level to apply to all containers. Ensure your container image supports running as a non-root user (many official images do).

## Learn More

See the Pod Security Standards Restricted profile and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.6. Running as non-root is a fundamental container security best practice.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.runAsNonRoot
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.1 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] psa-restricted-violations
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/default-sa-automount
  Container:   app
  Message:     Pod "default-sa-automount" container "app" violates PSS Restricted: allowPrivilegeEscalation is not false.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

When `allowPrivilegeEscalation` is true (the default), processes inside the container can gain more privileges than their parent process. This enables attacks via setuid/setgid binaries, kernel exploits, and other escalation vectors that can lead to container escape.

## How to Fix

Explicitly set `allowPrivilegeEscalation` to false in the container's security context:

```yaml
securityContext:
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  runAsNonRoot: true
  capabilities:
    drop: [ALL]
```

This prevents setuid binaries and other privilege escalation vectors from working inside the container.

## Learn More

See the Pod Security Standards Restricted profile and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.5. Disabling privilege escalation is required for PSS Restricted compliance.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.1 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] psa-restricted-violations
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/default-sa-automount
  Container:   app
  Message:     Pod "default-sa-automount" container "app" violates PSS Restricted: capabilities.drop does not include ALL.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

By default, containers receive a set of Linux capabilities that may be exploited for privilege escalation. Without explicitly dropping ALL capabilities, containers retain permissions like NET_RAW (enabling packet spoofing) and FOWNER (bypassing file permission checks).

## How to Fix

Drop all capabilities and add back only the specific ones your application requires:

```yaml
securityContext:
  capabilities:
    drop: [ALL]
    add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]  # Only if binding to ports below 1024
```

Most applications work correctly with all capabilities dropped. Test your workload first and add back only capabilities that cause failures.

## Learn More

See the Pod Security Standards Restricted profile and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.7. Dropping ALL capabilities is required for PSS Restricted compliance.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.capabilities.drop
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.1 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] read-only-rootfs
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/default-sa-automount
  Container:   app
  Message:     Container "app" does not have a read-only root filesystem.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

A writable root filesystem allows an attacker who gains code execution in your container to modify application binaries, install attack tools, plant backdoors, or persist malware across container restarts. Making the filesystem read-only eliminates an entire class of post-exploitation techniques.

## How to Fix

Enable a read-only root filesystem and mount writable volumes only where needed:

```yaml
securityContext:
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
volumeMounts:
  - name: tmp
    mountPath: /tmp
volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}
```

Common paths that need write access include /tmp, /var/cache, and /var/run. Mount each as an emptyDir or tmpfs volume rather than making the entire filesystem writable.

## Learn More

This aligns with CIS Benchmark 5.2.4 and the defense-in-depth principle. Combined with dropping capabilities and running as non-root, a read-only filesystem forms a strong container hardening baseline.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1565.001 · NSA 1.2

[Medium] resource-limits-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/default-sa-automount
  Container:   app
  Message:     Container "app" is missing both CPU and memory limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without resource limits, a single container can consume all available CPU and memory on a node, starving other workloads and triggering cascading failures. An attacker who compromises an unlimited container can mount a denial-of-service attack against the entire node with a simple fork bomb or memory allocation loop.

## How to Fix

Set both CPU and memory limits based on your application's actual resource usage:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 256Mi
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
```

Profile your application under load to determine appropriate values. Set limits to handle peak usage and requests to match steady-state consumption.

## Learn More

Use LimitRange objects to enforce default limits at the namespace level. Resource limits also determine the pod's QoS class: pods with equal requests and limits get Guaranteed QoS and are last to be evicted.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Medium] resource-requests-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/default-sa-automount
  Container:   app
  Message:     Container "app" is missing both CPU and memory requests.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Resource requests tell the Kubernetes scheduler how much CPU and memory your container needs. Without requests, the scheduler treats the pod as needing zero resources and may pack too many pods onto a single node. This leads to overcommitment, resource contention, throttling, and OOM kills under load.

## How to Fix

Set resource requests based on your application's steady-state usage:

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 256Mi
```

Observe your application's actual resource consumption using `kubectl top` or a monitoring tool, then set requests to match the typical steady-state usage.

## Learn More

Resource requests determine the pod's QoS class and scheduling behavior. Pods with requests equal to limits receive Guaranteed QoS. Use Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) to automatically recommend request values.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.requests
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Medium] run-as-group
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/default-sa-automount
  Container:   app
  Message:     Container "app" does not set runAsGroup; the process will run as GID 0 (root group) by default.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without an explicit runAsGroup, the container process defaults to GID 0 (the root group). Files and sockets owned by the root group become accessible to the container, including potentially sensitive host files if volumes are mounted. This widens the attack surface unnecessarily.

## How to Fix

Set an explicit non-root group in the securityContext:

```yaml
securityContext:
  runAsGroup: 1000
  runAsUser: 1000
  runAsNonRoot: true
```

Ensure the container image's application files and directories are readable by the specified GID. You may need to adjust file ownership in your Dockerfile with `chown`.

## Learn More

This aligns with CIS Benchmark 5.2.6 and the Pod Security Standards "Restricted" profile. Always set runAsUser, runAsGroup, and runAsNonRoot together for comprehensive identity control.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.runAsGroup
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.7 · MITRE T1068 · NSA 1.1

```yaml
  runAsUser: 1000
  runAsNonRoot: true
```

Ensure the container image's application files and directories are readable by the specified GID. You may need to adjust file ownership in your Dockerfile with `chown`.

## Learn More

This aligns with CIS Benchmark 5.2.6 and the Pod Security Standards "Restricted" profile. Always set runAsUser, runAsGroup, and runAsNonRoot together for comprehensive identity control.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.runAsGroup
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.7 · MITRE T1068 · NSA 1.1

[Medium] seccomp-profile
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/explicit-default-sa
  Container:   app
  Message:     Container "app" does not have a Seccomp profile set at either the container or pod level.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a Seccomp profile, containers can invoke any of the 300+ Linux system calls, leaving the entire kernel attack surface exposed. Kernel vulnerabilities in obscure syscalls are a primary vector for container escapes. Seccomp filtering blocks dangerous syscalls that legitimate applications never use.

## How to Fix

Apply a Seccomp profile at the container or pod level:

```yaml
securityContext:
  seccompProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
```

The RuntimeDefault profile blocks approximately 50 dangerous syscalls while allowing normal application behavior. For stricter controls, use a custom Localhost profile tailored to your application's needs. Set the profile at the pod level to apply it to all containers.

## Learn More

Seccomp profiles are required by the Pod Security Standards "Restricted" profile and CIS Benchmark 5.7.2. Use tools like `strace` or the Security Profiles Operator to generate custom profiles for your workloads.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.seccompProfile
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.2 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] apparmor-profile
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/explicit-root
  Container:   root-container
  Message:     Container "root-container" does not have an AppArmor profile set.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

AppArmor provides mandatory access control (MAC) that restricts which files, network resources, and capabilities a container process can access. Without an AppArmor profile, the container operates without these restrictions, allowing an attacker with code execution to access any file the container user can read and make unrestricted network connections.

## How to Fix

Apply an AppArmor profile in the container's securityContext (Kubernetes 1.30+):

```yaml
securityContext:
  appArmorProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
```

The RuntimeDefault profile provides sensible restrictions for most applications. For tighter control, create a custom Localhost profile that only allows the specific file and network access your application needs.

## Learn More

AppArmor is available on Debian/Ubuntu-based nodes. RHEL/CentOS nodes use SELinux instead. Both provide MAC enforcement. Refer to CIS Benchmark 5.7.5 and the Kubernetes AppArmor documentation.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.appArmorProfile
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] capabilities-not-dropped
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/explicit-root
  Container:   root-container
  Message:     Container "root-container" does not drop ALL capabilities, leaving it with unnecessary default privileges.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

By default, containers receive a set of Linux capabilities including KILL, SETUID, SETGID, and NET_RAW. These defaults are rarely needed by application code and significantly increase the potential damage from a container compromise. Dropping all capabilities follows the principle of least privilege.

## How to Fix

Explicitly drop all capabilities and selectively add back only what your application needs:

```yaml
securityContext:
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"]
    add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]  # Only if needed
```

Most web applications, API servers, and background workers run perfectly with all capabilities dropped. Test your application after making this change to confirm no functionality is lost.

## Learn More

This is required by the Pod Security Standards "Restricted" profile and aligns with CIS Benchmark 5.2.7. Kubernetes best practice is to treat capability grants as exceptions that require explicit justification.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.capabilities.drop
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.8 · CIS 5.2.10 · MITRE T1068 · NSA 1.1

[Medium] image-pull-policy
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/explicit-root
  Container:   root-container
  Message:     Container "root-container" uses a mutable image tag with pullPolicy "IfNotPresent" (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), risking stale images.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

When a mutable image tag is used without `imagePullPolicy: Always`, Kubernetes may serve a cached version of the image from the node. If the tag has been updated in the registry (with a security patch or -- worse -- a compromised layer), the running container will not reflect those changes.

## How to Fix

Set `imagePullPolicy: Always` for any container using a mutable tag:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:1.25.3
    imagePullPolicy: Always   # Forces fresh pull each time
```

Alternatively, pin images by digest (`image@sha256:...`), which makes the pull policy irrelevant because the content is immutable.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on image pull policies and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.4.2 for pull policy guidance.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].imagePullPolicy
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Medium] projected-volume-security
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/explicit-root
  Message:     Pod "explicit-root" has projected volume "kube-api-access-9z44q" with defaultMode 0644 which is too permissive.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Projected volumes with overly permissive file modes allow any process in the pod to read sensitive data such as service account tokens and secrets. If a container is compromised, the attacker can easily harvest these credentials to escalate privileges or move laterally within the cluster.

## How to Fix

Reduce the defaultMode to restrict file access:

```yaml
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: kube-api-access-9z44q
      projected:
        defaultMode: 0400         # Owner read-only (was too permissive)
        sources:
          - serviceAccountToken:
              path: token
```

Use 0400 for read-only access or 0600 if the application must write to the mounted files.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Projected Volumes documentation for defaultMode details. The CIS Benchmark recommends file modes of 0600 or lower for sensitive volume mounts to limit exposure within the pod.
  Field:       .spec.volumes[0].projected.defaultMode
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.4.1 · MITRE T1552 · NSA 5.1

[Medium] psa-restricted-violations
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/explicit-root
  Container:   root-container
  Message:     Pod "explicit-root" container "root-container" violates PSS Restricted: runAsNonRoot is not true.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Running as root inside a container means that any container escape vulnerability immediately grants root access on the host node. Even without an escape, root inside the container can modify sensitive files, install packages, and access capabilities that non-root users cannot.

## How to Fix

Set `runAsNonRoot: true` and specify a non-root user ID in the security context:

```yaml
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000
  runAsGroup: 1000
```

Set this at the pod level to apply to all containers. Ensure your container image supports running as a non-root user (many official images do).

## Learn More

See the Pod Security Standards Restricted profile and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.6. Running as non-root is a fundamental container security best practice.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.runAsNonRoot
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.1 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] psa-restricted-violations
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/explicit-root
  Container:   root-container
  Message:     Pod "explicit-root" container "root-container" violates PSS Restricted: allowPrivilegeEscalation is not false.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

When `allowPrivilegeEscalation` is true (the default), processes inside the container can gain more privileges than their parent process. This enables attacks via setuid/setgid binaries, kernel exploits, and other escalation vectors that can lead to container escape.

## How to Fix

Explicitly set `allowPrivilegeEscalation` to false in the container's security context:

```yaml
securityContext:
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  runAsNonRoot: true
  capabilities:
    drop: [ALL]
```

This prevents setuid binaries and other privilege escalation vectors from working inside the container.

## Learn More

See the Pod Security Standards Restricted profile and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.5. Disabling privilege escalation is required for PSS Restricted compliance.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.1 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] psa-restricted-violations
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/explicit-root
  Container:   root-container
  Message:     Pod "explicit-root" container "root-container" violates PSS Restricted: capabilities.drop does not include ALL.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

By default, containers receive a set of Linux capabilities that may be exploited for privilege escalation. Without explicitly dropping ALL capabilities, containers retain permissions like NET_RAW (enabling packet spoofing) and FOWNER (bypassing file permission checks).

## How to Fix

Drop all capabilities and add back only the specific ones your application requires:

```yaml
securityContext:
  capabilities:
    drop: [ALL]
    add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]  # Only if binding to ports below 1024
```

Most applications work correctly with all capabilities dropped. Test your workload first and add back only capabilities that cause failures.

## Learn More

See the Pod Security Standards Restricted profile and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.7. Dropping ALL capabilities is required for PSS Restricted compliance.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.capabilities.drop
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.1 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] read-only-rootfs
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/explicit-root
  Container:   root-container
  Message:     Container "root-container" does not have a read-only root filesystem.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

A writable root filesystem allows an attacker who gains code execution in your container to modify application binaries, install attack tools, plant backdoors, or persist malware across container restarts. Making the filesystem read-only eliminates an entire class of post-exploitation techniques.

## How to Fix

Enable a read-only root filesystem and mount writable volumes only where needed:

```yaml
securityContext:
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
volumeMounts:
  - name: tmp
    mountPath: /tmp
volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}
```

Common paths that need write access include /tmp, /var/cache, and /var/run. Mount each as an emptyDir or tmpfs volume rather than making the entire filesystem writable.

## Learn More

This aligns with CIS Benchmark 5.2.4 and the defense-in-depth principle. Combined with dropping capabilities and running as non-root, a read-only filesystem forms a strong container hardening baseline.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1565.001 · NSA 1.2

[Medium] resource-limits-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/explicit-root
  Container:   root-container
  Message:     Container "root-container" is missing both CPU and memory limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without resource limits, a single container can consume all available CPU and memory on a node, starving other workloads and triggering cascading failures. An attacker who compromises an unlimited container can mount a denial-of-service attack against the entire node with a simple fork bomb or memory allocation loop.

## How to Fix

Set both CPU and memory limits based on your application's actual resource usage:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 256Mi
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
```

Profile your application under load to determine appropriate values. Set limits to handle peak usage and requests to match steady-state consumption.

## Learn More

Use LimitRange objects to enforce default limits at the namespace level. Resource limits also determine the pod's QoS class: pods with equal requests and limits get Guaranteed QoS and are last to be evicted.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Medium] resource-requests-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/explicit-root
  Container:   root-container
  Message:     Container "root-container" is missing both CPU and memory requests.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Resource requests tell the Kubernetes scheduler how much CPU and memory your container needs. Without requests, the scheduler treats the pod as needing zero resources and may pack too many pods onto a single node. This leads to overcommitment, resource contention, throttling, and OOM kills under load.

## How to Fix

Set resource requests based on your application's steady-state usage:

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 256Mi
```

Observe your application's actual resource consumption using `kubectl top` or a monitoring tool, then set requests to match the typical steady-state usage.

## Learn More

Resource requests determine the pod's QoS class and scheduling behavior. Pods with requests equal to limits receive Guaranteed QoS. Use Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) to automatically recommend request values.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.requests
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Medium] run-as-group
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/explicit-root
  Container:   root-container
  Message:     Container "root-container" is explicitly configured to run as the root group (GID 0).
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Explicitly setting runAsGroup to 0 runs the container as the root group, granting access to any files and resources owned by GID 0. This includes many system files on the host if volumes are mounted, and it increases the potential damage from a container compromise or escape.

## How to Fix

```yaml
securityContext:

  runAsUser: 1000
  runAsNonRoot: true
```

## Learn More

This aligns with CIS Benchmark 5.2.6 and the Pod Security Standards "Restricted" profile. Always set runAsUser, runAsGroup, and runAsNonRoot together for comprehensive identity control.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.runAsGroup
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.7 · MITRE T1068 · NSA 1.1

[Medium] seccomp-profile
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/host-ipc-pod
  Container:   ipc-container
  Message:     Container "ipc-container" does not have a Seccomp profile set at either the container or pod level.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a Seccomp profile, containers can invoke any of the 300+ Linux system calls, leaving the entire kernel attack surface exposed. Kernel vulnerabilities in obscure syscalls are a primary vector for container escapes. Seccomp filtering blocks dangerous syscalls that legitimate applications never use.

## How to Fix

Apply a Seccomp profile at the container or pod level:

```yaml
securityContext:
  seccompProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
```

The RuntimeDefault profile blocks approximately 50 dangerous syscalls while allowing normal application behavior. For stricter controls, use a custom Localhost profile tailored to your application's needs. Set the profile at the pod level to apply it to all containers.

## Learn More

Seccomp profiles are required by the Pod Security Standards "Restricted" profile and CIS Benchmark 5.7.2. Use tools like `strace` or the Security Profiles Operator to generate custom profiles for your workloads.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.seccompProfile
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.2 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] apparmor-profile
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/host-network-pod
  Container:   network-container
  Message:     Container "network-container" does not have an AppArmor profile set.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

AppArmor provides mandatory access control (MAC) that restricts which files, network resources, and capabilities a container process can access. Without an AppArmor profile, the container operates without these restrictions, allowing an attacker with code execution to access any file the container user can read and make unrestricted network connections.

## How to Fix

Apply an AppArmor profile in the container's securityContext (Kubernetes 1.30+):

```yaml
securityContext:
  appArmorProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
```

The RuntimeDefault profile provides sensible restrictions for most applications. For tighter control, create a custom Localhost profile that only allows the specific file and network access your application needs.

## Learn More

AppArmor is available on Debian/Ubuntu-based nodes. RHEL/CentOS nodes use SELinux instead. Both provide MAC enforcement. Refer to CIS Benchmark 5.7.5 and the Kubernetes AppArmor documentation.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.appArmorProfile
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] capabilities-not-dropped
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/host-network-pod
  Container:   network-container
  Message:     Container "network-container" does not drop ALL capabilities, leaving it with unnecessary default privileges.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

By default, containers receive a set of Linux capabilities including KILL, SETUID, SETGID, and NET_RAW. These defaults are rarely needed by application code and significantly increase the potential damage from a container compromise. Dropping all capabilities follows the principle of least privilege.

## How to Fix

Explicitly drop all capabilities and selectively add back only what your application needs:

```yaml
securityContext:
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"]
    add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]  # Only if needed
```

Most web applications, API servers, and background workers run perfectly with all capabilities dropped. Test your application after making this change to confirm no functionality is lost.

## Learn More

This is required by the Pod Security Standards "Restricted" profile and aligns with CIS Benchmark 5.2.7. Kubernetes best practice is to treat capability grants as exceptions that require explicit justification.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.capabilities.drop
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.8 · CIS 5.2.10 · MITRE T1068 · NSA 1.1

[Medium] image-pull-policy
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/host-network-pod
  Container:   network-container
  Message:     Container "network-container" uses a mutable image tag with pullPolicy "IfNotPresent" (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), risking stale images.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

When a mutable image tag is used without `imagePullPolicy: Always`, Kubernetes may serve a cached version of the image from the node. If the tag has been updated in the registry (with a security patch or -- worse -- a compromised layer), the running container will not reflect those changes.

## How to Fix

Set `imagePullPolicy: Always` for any container using a mutable tag:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:1.25.3
    imagePullPolicy: Always   # Forces fresh pull each time
```

Alternatively, pin images by digest (`image@sha256:...`), which makes the pull policy irrelevant because the content is immutable.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on image pull policies and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.4.2 for pull policy guidance.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].imagePullPolicy
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Medium] projected-volume-security
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/host-network-pod
  Message:     Pod "host-network-pod" has projected volume "kube-api-access-mx28r" with defaultMode 0644 which is too permissive.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Projected volumes with overly permissive file modes allow any process in the pod to read sensitive data such as service account tokens and secrets. If a container is compromised, the attacker can easily harvest these credentials to escalate privileges or move laterally within the cluster.

## How to Fix

Reduce the defaultMode to restrict file access:

```yaml
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: kube-api-access-mx28r
      projected:
        defaultMode: 0400         # Owner read-only (was too permissive)
        sources:
          - serviceAccountToken:
              path: token
```

Use 0400 for read-only access or 0600 if the application must write to the mounted files.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Projected Volumes documentation for defaultMode details. The CIS Benchmark recommends file modes of 0600 or lower for sensitive volume mounts to limit exposure within the pod.
  Field:       .spec.volumes[0].projected.defaultMode
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.4.1 · MITRE T1552 · NSA 5.1

[Medium] psa-restricted-violations
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/host-network-pod
  Container:   network-container
  Message:     Pod "host-network-pod" container "network-container" violates PSS Restricted: runAsNonRoot is not true.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Running as root inside a container means that any container escape vulnerability immediately grants root access on the host node. Even without an escape, root inside the container can modify sensitive files, install packages, and access capabilities that non-root users cannot.

## How to Fix

Set `runAsNonRoot: true` and specify a non-root user ID in the security context:

```yaml
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000
  runAsGroup: 1000
```

Set this at the pod level to apply to all containers. Ensure your container image supports running as a non-root user (many official images do).

## Learn More

See the Pod Security Standards Restricted profile and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.6. Running as non-root is a fundamental container security best practice.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.runAsNonRoot
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.1 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] psa-restricted-violations
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/host-network-pod
  Container:   network-container
  Message:     Pod "host-network-pod" container "network-container" violates PSS Restricted: allowPrivilegeEscalation is not false.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

When `allowPrivilegeEscalation` is true (the default), processes inside the container can gain more privileges than their parent process. This enables attacks via setuid/setgid binaries, kernel exploits, and other escalation vectors that can lead to container escape.

## How to Fix

Explicitly set `allowPrivilegeEscalation` to false in the container's security context:

```yaml
securityContext:
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  runAsNonRoot: true
  capabilities:
    drop: [ALL]
```

This prevents setuid binaries and other privilege escalation vectors from working inside the container.

## Learn More

See the Pod Security Standards Restricted profile and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.5. Disabling privilege escalation is required for PSS Restricted compliance.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.1 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] psa-restricted-violations
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/host-network-pod
  Container:   network-container
  Message:     Pod "host-network-pod" container "network-container" violates PSS Restricted: capabilities.drop does not include ALL.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

By default, containers receive a set of Linux capabilities that may be exploited for privilege escalation. Without explicitly dropping ALL capabilities, containers retain permissions like NET_RAW (enabling packet spoofing) and FOWNER (bypassing file permission checks).

## How to Fix

Drop all capabilities and add back only the specific ones your application requires:

```yaml
securityContext:
  capabilities:
    drop: [ALL]
    add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]  # Only if binding to ports below 1024
```

Most applications work correctly with all capabilities dropped. Test your workload first and add back only capabilities that cause failures.

## Learn More

See the Pod Security Standards Restricted profile and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.7. Dropping ALL capabilities is required for PSS Restricted compliance.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.capabilities.drop
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.1 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Medium] read-only-rootfs
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/host-network-pod
  Container:   network-container
  Message:     Container "network-container" does not have a read-only root filesystem.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

A writable root filesystem allows an attacker who gains code execution in your container to modify application binaries, install attack tools, plant backdoors, or persist malware across container restarts. Making the filesystem read-only eliminates an entire class of post-exploitation techniques.

## How to Fix

Enable a read-only root filesystem and mount writable volumes only where needed:

```yaml
securityContext:
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
volumeMounts:
  - name: tmp
    mountPath: /tmp
volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}
```

Common paths that need write access include /tmp, /var/cache, and /var/run. Mount each as an emptyDir or tmpfs volume rather than making the entire filesystem writable.

## Learn More

This aligns with CIS Benchmark 5.2.4 and the defense-in-depth principle. Combined with dropping capabilities and running as non-root, a read-only filesystem forms a strong container hardening baseline.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1565.001 · NSA 1.2

[Medium] resource-limits-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/host-network-pod
  Container:   network-container
  Message:     Container "network-container" is missing both CPU and memory limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without resource limits, a single container can consume all available CPU and memory on a node, starving other workloads and triggering cascading failures. An attacker who compromises an unlimited container can mount a denial-of-service attack against the entire node with a simple fork bomb or memory allocation loop.

## How to Fix

Set both CPU and memory limits based on your application's actual resource usage:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 256Mi
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
```

Profile your application under load to determine appropriate values. Set limits to handle peak usage and requests to match steady-state consumption.

## Learn More

Use LimitRange objects to enforce default limits at the namespace level. Resource limits also determine the pod's QoS class: pods with equal requests and limits get Guaranteed QoS and are last to be evicted.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Medium] resource-requests-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/host-network-pod
  Container:   network-container
  Message:     Container "network-container" is missing both CPU and memory requests.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Resource requests tell the Kubernetes scheduler how much CPU and memory your container needs. Without requests, the scheduler treats the pod as needing zero resources and may pack too many pods onto a single node. This leads to overcommitment, resource contention, throttling, and OOM kills under load.

## How to Fix

Set resource requests based on your application's steady-state usage:

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 256Mi
```

Observe your application's actual resource consumption using `kubectl top` or a monitoring tool, then set requests to match the typical steady-state usage.

## Learn More

Resource requests determine the pod's QoS class and scheduling behavior. Pods with requests equal to limits receive Guaranteed QoS. Use Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) to automatically recommend request values.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.requests
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5
