  Message:     Container "implicit-latest" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[1].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-image/Deployment/latest-tag-demo
  Container:   implicit-latest
  Message:     Container "implicit-latest" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[1].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-image/Deployment/latest-tag-demo
  Message:     Deployment "latest-tag-demo" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-image/Deployment/latest-tag-demo
  Message:     Pod "latest-tag-demo" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-image/Deployment/latest-tag-demo
  Message:     Deployment "latest-tag-demo" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-image/Deployment/mixed-images-demo
  Container:   app-mutable
  Message:     Container "app-mutable" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-image/Deployment/mixed-images-demo
  Container:   app-mutable
  Message:     Container "app-mutable" image is not pinned by digest (image: nginx:1.25), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

```yaml
resources:

    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-image/Deployment/no-digest-demo
  Container:   tag-only
  Message:     Container "tag-only" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-image/Deployment/no-digest-demo
  Container:   tag-only
  Message:     Container "tag-only" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-image/Deployment/no-digest-demo
  Message:     Deployment "no-digest-demo" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-image/Deployment/no-digest-demo
  Message:     Pod "no-digest-demo" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-image/Deployment/no-digest-demo
  Message:     Deployment "no-digest-demo" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-image/Deployment/pull-policy-demo
  Container:   latest-default
  Message:     Container "latest-default" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[3].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-image/Deployment/pull-policy-demo
  Container:   latest-default
  Message:     Container "latest-default" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[3].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-image/Deployment/pull-policy-demo
  Message:     Deployment "pull-policy-demo" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-image/Deployment/pull-policy-demo
  Message:     Pod "pull-policy-demo" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-image/Deployment/pull-policy-demo
  Message:     Deployment "pull-policy-demo" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Deployment/backend
  Container:   api
  Message:     Container "api" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Deployment/backend
  Container:   api
  Message:     Container "api" image is not pinned by digest (image: busybox:1.36), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Low] pod-disruption-budget
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Deployment/backend
  Message:     Deployment "backend" has 2 replicas but no matching PodDisruptionBudget; all replicas can be evicted simultaneously.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PodDisruptionBudget, Kubernetes can evict all replicas of your workload simultaneously during voluntary disruptions like node drains, cluster upgrades, or autoscaler scale-downs. This causes complete service downtime even though you have multiple replicas.

## How to Fix

Create a PodDisruptionBudget that matches your workload's pod labels:

```yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: my-app-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 1              # Or use maxUnavailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app              # Must match your Deployment/StatefulSet pod labels
```

Use `minAvailable` to guarantee a minimum number of running pods, or `maxUnavailable` to limit how many can be down at once.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes PodDisruptionBudget documentation for details on voluntary disruption handling. PDBs are essential for production workloads that need high availability during cluster maintenance.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] run-as-high-uid
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Deployment/database
  Container:   postgres
  Message:     Container "postgres" runs as UID 999, which is below the recommended minimum of 10000.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

UIDs below 10000 overlap with well-known system accounts on most Linux distributions (e.g., daemon, www-data, nobody). If a container running with a low UID escapes to the host, it may inherit the permissions of that system account, gaining unintended access to host files, sockets, or services owned by that UID.

## How to Fix

Use a high UID that does not overlap with host system accounts:

```yaml
securityContext:
  runAsUser: 65534       # nobody, or any UID >= 10000
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsGroup: 65534
```

Choose a UID >= 10000. The conventional `nobody` UID (65534) is a safe default. Also set the UID in your Dockerfile with `USER 65534` for defense in depth.

## Learn More

This is a defense-in-depth measure. While container UID mapping varies by runtime, using high UIDs avoids accidental privilege overlap on hosts that lack user namespace remapping.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.runAsUser
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.7 · MITRE T1068 · NSA 1.1

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Deployment/database
  Message:     Pod "database" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Deployment/database
  Message:     Deployment "database" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Deployment/frontend
  Container:   nginx
  Message:     Container "nginx" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Deployment/frontend
  Container:   nginx
  Message:     Container "nginx" image is not pinned by digest (image: nginx:latest), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Deployment/frontend
  Container:   nginx
  Message:     Container "nginx" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Deployment/frontend
  Container:   nginx
  Message:     Container "nginx" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] pod-disruption-budget
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Deployment/frontend
  Message:     Deployment "frontend" has 2 replicas but no matching PodDisruptionBudget; all replicas can be evicted simultaneously.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PodDisruptionBudget, Kubernetes can evict all replicas of your workload simultaneously during voluntary disruptions like node drains, cluster upgrades, or autoscaler scale-downs. This causes complete service downtime even though you have multiple replicas.

## How to Fix

Create a PodDisruptionBudget that matches your workload's pod labels:

```yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: my-app-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 1              # Or use maxUnavailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app              # Must match your Deployment/StatefulSet pod labels
```

Use `minAvailable` to guarantee a minimum number of running pods, or `maxUnavailable` to limit how many can be down at once.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes PodDisruptionBudget documentation for details on voluntary disruption handling. PDBs are essential for production workloads that need high availability during cluster maintenance.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing

[Low] limit-range-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Namespace/kv-e2e-mixed
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-mixed" has no LimitRange defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a LimitRange, any container can be created without resource constraints. A single runaway or malicious pod can consume all node CPU and memory, causing denial of service for other workloads on the same node.

## How to Fix

Create a LimitRange in the namespace to set default and maximum resource constraints:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 256Mi
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      max:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 1Gi
```

Containers that omit resource requests/limits will inherit these defaults automatically.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.1 recommends LimitRanges for resource governance. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/limit-range/ for configuration details.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] resource-quota-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Namespace/kv-e2e-mixed
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-mixed" has no ResourceQuota defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a ResourceQuota, a single namespace can consume the entire cluster's CPU, memory, and storage. This creates a noisy-neighbor problem where one team's workloads starve others, and makes capacity planning impossible.

## How to Fix

Create a ResourceQuota to cap the namespace's total resource consumption:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-quota
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "10"
    requests.memory: 20Gi
    limits.cpu: "20"
    limits.memory: 40Gi
    pods: "50"
    services: "10"
```

Tune quota values based on the namespace's actual workload requirements and cluster capacity.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.2 recommends ResourceQuotas for multi-tenant clusters. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/ for quota configuration and enforcement behavior.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] emptydir-size-limit
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Deployment/partially-hardened-app
  Message:     Deployment "partially-hardened-app" has emptyDir volume "tmp" without sizeLimit; a container can fill the node disk.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

An emptyDir volume without a sizeLimit allows a container to write unlimited data to the node's filesystem. A compromised or misbehaving container can fill the entire node disk, causing kubelet failures, pod evictions, and node instability that affects all workloads on that node.

## How to Fix

Set a sizeLimit on the emptyDir volume based on expected usage:

```yaml
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: tmp
      emptyDir:
        sizeLimit: 1Gi           # Set to expected max usage
        medium: ""               # Or Memory for tmpfs
```

When the limit is exceeded, the pod will be evicted. Size conservatively and monitor actual usage to tune the limit.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Volumes documentation on emptyDir. Setting sizeLimit is a defense-in-depth measure that protects node stability alongside resource quotas and LimitRanges.

  Container:   web
  Message:     Container "web" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] pod-disruption-budget
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Deployment/startup-web-app
  Message:     Deployment "startup-web-app" has 2 replicas but no matching PodDisruptionBudget; all replicas can be evicted simultaneously.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PodDisruptionBudget, Kubernetes can evict all replicas of your workload simultaneously during voluntary disruptions like node drains, cluster upgrades, or autoscaler scale-downs. This causes complete service downtime even though you have multiple replicas.

## How to Fix

Create a PodDisruptionBudget that matches your workload's pod labels:

```yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: my-app-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 1              # Or use maxUnavailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app              # Must match your Deployment/StatefulSet pod labels
```

Use `minAvailable` to guarantee a minimum number of running pods, or `maxUnavailable` to limit how many can be down at once.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes PodDisruptionBudget documentation for details on voluntary disruption handling. PDBs are essential for production workloads that need high availability during cluster maintenance.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Deployment/startup-web-app
  Message:     Deployment "startup-web-app" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Deployment/startup-web-app
  Message:     Pod "startup-web-app" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-mixed/Deployment/startup-web-app
  Message:     Deployment "startup-web-app" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] limit-range-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-network/Namespace/kv-e2e-network
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-network" has no LimitRange defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a LimitRange, any container can be created without resource constraints. A single runaway or malicious pod can consume all node CPU and memory, causing denial of service for other workloads on the same node.

## How to Fix

Create a LimitRange in the namespace to set default and maximum resource constraints:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 256Mi
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      max:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 1Gi
```

Containers that omit resource requests/limits will inherit these defaults automatically.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.1 recommends LimitRanges for resource governance. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/limit-range/ for configuration details.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] resource-quota-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-network/Namespace/kv-e2e-network
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-network" has no ResourceQuota defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a ResourceQuota, a single namespace can consume the entire cluster's CPU, memory, and storage. This creates a noisy-neighbor problem where one team's workloads starve others, and makes capacity planning impossible.

## How to Fix

Create a ResourceQuota to cap the namespace's total resource consumption:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-quota
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "10"
    requests.memory: 20Gi
    limits.cpu: "20"
    limits.memory: 40Gi
    pods: "50"
    services: "10"
```

Tune quota values based on the namespace's actual workload requirements and cluster capacity.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.2 recommends ResourceQuotas for multi-tenant clusters. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/ for quota configuration and enforcement behavior.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ingress-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-network/Ingress/no-class-ingress
  Message:     Ingress "no-class-ingress" has no ingressClassName or ingress.class annotation. It may not be handled by any ingress controller.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without an explicit IngressClass, this Ingress relies on the cluster's default ingress controller. If no default is configured, the Ingress may be silently ignored. If multiple controllers exist, the wrong one may claim it, leading to misrouted traffic or missing security configurations like WAF rules and rate limiting.

## How to Fix

Set the `ingressClassName` field to explicitly declare which controller should handle this Ingress:

```yaml
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
    - host: app.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: app
                port:
                  number: 80
```

List available IngressClasses with `kubectl get ingressclass` to find the correct class name.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes IngressClass documentation. The deprecated `kubernetes.io/ingress.class` annotation is still supported but `spec.ingressClassName` is the preferred approach in Kubernetes 1.18+.
  Field:       .spec.ingressClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.3.2 · MITRE T1190 · NSA 4.1

[Low] ingress-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-network/Ingress/no-tls-ingress
  Message:     Ingress "no-tls-ingress" has no ingressClassName or ingress.class annotation. It may not be handled by any ingress controller.

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-network/Deployment/pause-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-network/Deployment/pause-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" image is not pinned by digest (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-network/Deployment/pause-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-network-deny/Deployment/web
  Message:     Pod "web" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-network-deny/Deployment/web
  Message:     Deployment "web" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] limit-range-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa/Namespace/kv-e2e-psa
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-psa" has no LimitRange defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a LimitRange, any container can be created without resource constraints. A single runaway or malicious pod can consume all node CPU and memory, causing denial of service for other workloads on the same node.

## How to Fix

Create a LimitRange in the namespace to set default and maximum resource constraints:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 256Mi
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      max:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 1Gi
```

Containers that omit resource requests/limits will inherit these defaults automatically.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.1 recommends LimitRanges for resource governance. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/limit-range/ for configuration details.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] resource-quota-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa/Namespace/kv-e2e-psa
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-psa" has no ResourceQuota defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a ResourceQuota, a single namespace can consume the entire cluster's CPU, memory, and storage. This creates a noisy-neighbor problem where one team's workloads starve others, and makes capacity planning impossible.

## How to Fix

Create a ResourceQuota to cap the namespace's total resource consumption:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-quota
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "10"
    requests.memory: 20Gi
    limits.cpu: "20"
    limits.memory: 40Gi
    pods: "50"
    services: "10"
```

Tune quota values based on the namespace's actual workload requirements and cluster capacity.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.2 recommends ResourceQuotas for multi-tenant clusters. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/ for quota configuration and enforcement behavior.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa/Deployment/unprotected-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa/Deployment/unprotected-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" image is not pinned by digest (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa/Deployment/unprotected-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa/Deployment/unprotected-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa/Deployment/unprotected-app
  Message:     Deployment "unprotected-app" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-baseline/Deployment/dangerous-caps-app
  Message:     Pod "dangerous-caps-app" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-baseline/Deployment/dangerous-caps-app
  Message:     Deployment "dangerous-caps-app" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-baseline/Deployment/host-network-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-baseline/Deployment/host-network-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" image is not pinned by digest (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-baseline/Deployment/host-network-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-baseline/Deployment/host-network-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] limit-range-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-baseline/Namespace/kv-e2e-psa-baseline
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-psa-baseline" has no LimitRange defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a LimitRange, any container can be created without resource constraints. A single runaway or malicious pod can consume all node CPU and memory, causing denial of service for other workloads on the same node.

## How to Fix

Create a LimitRange in the namespace to set default and maximum resource constraints:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 256Mi
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      max:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 1Gi
```

Containers that omit resource requests/limits will inherit these defaults automatically.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.1 recommends LimitRanges for resource governance. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/limit-range/ for configuration details.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] resource-quota-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-baseline/Namespace/kv-e2e-psa-baseline
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-psa-baseline" has no ResourceQuota defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a ResourceQuota, a single namespace can consume the entire cluster's CPU, memory, and storage. This creates a noisy-neighbor problem where one team's workloads starve others, and makes capacity planning impossible.

## How to Fix

Create a ResourceQuota to cap the namespace's total resource consumption:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-quota
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "10"
    requests.memory: 20Gi
    limits.cpu: "20"
    limits.memory: 40Gi
    pods: "50"
    services: "10"
```

Tune quota values based on the namespace's actual workload requirements and cluster capacity.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.2 recommends ResourceQuotas for multi-tenant clusters. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/ for quota configuration and enforcement behavior.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-pinned/Deployment/compliant-app
  Message:     Deployment "compliant-app" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] limit-range-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-pinned/Namespace/kv-e2e-psa-pinned
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-psa-pinned" has no LimitRange defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a LimitRange, any container can be created without resource constraints. A single runaway or malicious pod can consume all node CPU and memory, causing denial of service for other workloads on the same node.

## How to Fix

Create a LimitRange in the namespace to set default and maximum resource constraints:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 256Mi
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      max:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 1Gi
```

Containers that omit resource requests/limits will inherit these defaults automatically.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.1 recommends LimitRanges for resource governance. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/limit-range/ for configuration details.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] psa-version-pinning
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-pinned/Namespace/kv-e2e-psa-pinned
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-psa-pinned" has PSA version label pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version pinned to "v1.25" instead of "latest"; new restrictions won't apply on upgrade.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

When a PSA version label is pinned to a specific Kubernetes version, the namespace will not automatically benefit from new security restrictions added in later versions. After a cluster upgrade, workloads may be allowed to run configurations that the newer Pod Security Standards would otherwise block.

## How to Fix

Set the version label to "latest" so it always uses the security standards matching the current cluster version:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: my-namespace
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: "latest"
```

If pinning is intentional (e.g., for compatibility testing), document the reason and plan to update after validation.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Security Admission documentation on version labels. Using "latest" ensures your namespaces always apply the most up-to-date Pod Security Standards for the cluster version.
  Field:       .metadata.labels[pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version]
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.1 · MITRE T1610 · NSA 2.1
