[Low] resource-quota-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-pinned/Namespace/kv-e2e-psa-pinned
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-psa-pinned" has no ResourceQuota defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a ResourceQuota, a single namespace can consume the entire cluster's CPU, memory, and storage. This creates a noisy-neighbor problem where one team's workloads starve others, and makes capacity planning impossible.

## How to Fix

Create a ResourceQuota to cap the namespace's total resource consumption:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-quota
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "10"
    requests.memory: 20Gi
    limits.cpu: "20"
    limits.memory: 40Gi
    pods: "50"
    services: "10"
```

Tune quota values based on the namespace's actual workload requirements and cluster capacity.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.2 recommends ResourceQuotas for multi-tenant clusters. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/ for quota configuration and enforcement behavior.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-restricted/Deployment/explicit-root-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-restricted/Deployment/explicit-root-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" image is not pinned by digest (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-restricted/Deployment/explicit-root-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-restricted/Deployment/explicit-root-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-restricted/Deployment/explicit-root-app
  Message:     Deployment "explicit-root-app" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-restricted/Deployment/partial-restricted-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" image is not pinned by digest (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-restricted/Deployment/partial-restricted-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-restricted/Deployment/partial-restricted-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-restricted/Deployment/partial-restricted-app
  Message:     Deployment "partial-restricted-app" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-restricted/Deployment/partial-restricted-app
  Message:     Pod "partial-restricted-app" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-psa-restricted/Deployment/partial-restricted-app
  Message:     Deployment "partial-restricted-app" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-rbac/Pod/kv-e2e-automount-pod
  Container:   app
  Message:     Container "app" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage

[Low] limit-range-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-rbac/Namespace/kv-e2e-rbac
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-rbac" has no LimitRange defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a LimitRange, any container can be created without resource constraints. A single runaway or malicious pod can consume all node CPU and memory, causing denial of service for other workloads on the same node.

## How to Fix

Create a LimitRange in the namespace to set default and maximum resource constraints:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 256Mi
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      max:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 1Gi
```

Containers that omit resource requests/limits will inherit these defaults automatically.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.1 recommends LimitRanges for resource governance. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/limit-range/ for configuration details.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] resource-quota-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-rbac/Namespace/kv-e2e-rbac
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-rbac" has no ResourceQuota defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a ResourceQuota, a single namespace can consume the entire cluster's CPU, memory, and storage. This creates a noisy-neighbor problem where one team's workloads starve others, and makes capacity planning impossible.

## How to Fix

Create a ResourceQuota to cap the namespace's total resource consumption:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-quota
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "10"
    requests.memory: 20Gi
    limits.cpu: "20"
    limits.memory: 40Gi
    pods: "50"
    services: "10"
```

Tune quota values based on the namespace's actual workload requirements and cluster capacity.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.2 recommends ResourceQuotas for multi-tenant clusters. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/ for quota configuration and enforcement behavior.

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/control-plane-tolerator
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/control-plane-tolerator
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/control-plane-tolerator
  Message:     Deployment "control-plane-tolerator" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/control-plane-tolerator
  Message:     Pod "control-plane-tolerator" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/control-plane-tolerator
  Message:     Deployment "control-plane-tolerator" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/hpa-target-no-requests
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/hpa-target-no-requests
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" image is not pinned by digest (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Low] pod-disruption-budget
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/hpa-target-no-requests
  Message:     Deployment "hpa-target-no-requests" has 2 replicas but no matching PodDisruptionBudget; all replicas can be evicted simultaneously.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

```yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: my-app-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 1              # Or use maxUnavailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app              # Must match your Deployment/StatefulSet pod labels
```

Use `minAvailable` to guarantee a minimum number of running pods, or `maxUnavailable` to limit how many can be down at once.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes PodDisruptionBudget documentation for details on voluntary disruption handling. PDBs are essential for production workloads that need high availability during cluster maintenance.

[Low] limit-range-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Namespace/kv-e2e-scheduling
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-scheduling" has no LimitRange defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a LimitRange, any container can be created without resource constraints. A single runaway or malicious pod can consume all node CPU and memory, causing denial of service for other workloads on the same node.

## How to Fix

Create a LimitRange in the namespace to set default and maximum resource constraints:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 256Mi
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      max:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 1Gi
```

Containers that omit resource requests/limits will inherit these defaults automatically.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.1 recommends LimitRanges for resource governance. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/limit-range/ for configuration details.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] resource-quota-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Namespace/kv-e2e-scheduling
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-scheduling" has no ResourceQuota defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a ResourceQuota, a single namespace can consume the entire cluster's CPU, memory, and storage. This creates a noisy-neighbor problem where one team's workloads starve others, and makes capacity planning impossible.

## How to Fix

Create a ResourceQuota to cap the namespace's total resource consumption:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-quota
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "10"
    requests.memory: 20Gi
    limits.cpu: "20"
    limits.memory: 40Gi
    pods: "50"
    services: "10"
```

Tune quota values based on the namespace's actual workload requirements and cluster capacity.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.2 recommends ResourceQuotas for multi-tenant clusters. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/ for quota configuration and enforcement behavior.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/no-priority-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" image is not pinned by digest (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/no-priority-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/no-priority-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/no-priority-app
  Message:     Deployment "no-priority-app" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/no-priority-app
  Message:     Pod "no-priority-app" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/no-priority-app
  Message:     Deployment "no-priority-app" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/no-topology-spread-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] pod-disruption-budget
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/no-topology-spread-app
  Message:     Deployment "no-topology-spread-app" has 3 replicas but no matching PodDisruptionBudget; all replicas can be evicted simultaneously.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

```yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1

metadata:
  name: my-app-pdb
spec:

  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app              # Must match your Deployment/StatefulSet pod labels
```

Use `minAvailable` to guarantee a minimum number of running pods, or `maxUnavailable` to limit how many can be down at once.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes PodDisruptionBudget documentation for details on voluntary disruption handling. PDBs are essential for production workloads that need high availability during cluster maintenance.

  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/spot-selector-deploy
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/spot-selector-deploy
  Message:     Deployment "spot-selector-deploy" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/spot-selector-deploy
  Message:     Pod "spot-selector-deploy" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/spot-selector-deploy
  Message:     Deployment "spot-selector-deploy" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/system-priority-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-scheduling/Deployment/system-priority-app
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" image is not pinned by digest (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

```yaml
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080

      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-secrets/Pod/app-with-secret-env
  Container:   app
  Message:     Container "app" image is not pinned by digest (image: nginx:1.25), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-secrets/Pod/app-with-secret-env
  Container:   app
  Message:     Container "app" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-secrets/Pod/app-with-secret-env
  Container:   app
  Message:     Container "app" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-secrets/Pod/app-with-secret-env
  Message:     Pod "app-with-secret-env" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-secrets/Pod/app-with-secret-env
  Message:     Pod "app-with-secret-env" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-secrets/Pod/app-with-secret-env
  Message:     Pod "app-with-secret-env" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] secrets-default-type
  Resource:    kv-e2e-secrets/Secret/db-auth-opaque

  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Kubernetes provides built-in Secret types (e.g., kubernetes.io/tls, kubernetes.io/basic-auth) that enforce required key names and enable automatic validation. Using the generic Opaque type bypasses these guardrails, making misconfigurations harder to catch and reducing interoperability with tools like cert-manager, Ingress controllers, and kubectl.

## How to Fix

Change the Secret type to the recommended built-in type:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: my-secret
type: kubernetes.io/basic-auth    # Use the specific type
```

Kubernetes will validate that the required data keys are present for the chosen type.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Secret types documentation for the full list of built-in types and their required keys. CIS Benchmark recommends using typed secrets for better auditability.
  Field:       .type
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.4.1 · MITRE T1552 · NSA 5.1

[Low] limit-range-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-secrets/Namespace/kv-e2e-secrets
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-secrets" has no LimitRange defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a LimitRange, any container can be created without resource constraints. A single runaway or malicious pod can consume all node CPU and memory, causing denial of service for other workloads on the same node.

## How to Fix

Create a LimitRange in the namespace to set default and maximum resource constraints:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 256Mi
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      max:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 1Gi
```

Containers that omit resource requests/limits will inherit these defaults automatically.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.1 recommends LimitRanges for resource governance. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/limit-range/ for configuration details.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] resource-quota-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-secrets/Namespace/kv-e2e-secrets
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-secrets" has no ResourceQuota defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a ResourceQuota, a single namespace can consume the entire cluster's CPU, memory, and storage. This creates a noisy-neighbor problem where one team's workloads starve others, and makes capacity planning impossible.

## How to Fix

Create a ResourceQuota to cap the namespace's total resource consumption:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-quota
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "10"
    requests.memory: 20Gi
    limits.cpu: "20"
    limits.memory: 40Gi
    pods: "50"
    services: "10"
```

Tune quota values based on the namespace's actual workload requirements and cluster capacity.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.2 recommends ResourceQuotas for multi-tenant clusters. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/ for quota configuration and enforcement behavior.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

```yaml
spec:
```

When the limit is exceeded, the pod will be evicted. Size conservatively and monitor actual usage to tune the limit.

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" image is not pinned by digest (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Container:   pause
  Message:     Container "pause" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Message:     Pod "projected-permissive" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Message:     Pod "projected-permissive" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-storage/Pod/projected-permissive
  Message:     Pod "projected-permissive" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/dangerous-capabilities
  Container:   caps-sys-admin
  Message:     Container "caps-sys-admin" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/default-sa-automount
  Container:   app
  Message:     Container "app" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/default-sa-automount
  Message:     Pod "default-sa-automount" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/default-sa-automount
  Message:     Pod "default-sa-automount" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/default-sa-automount
  Message:     Pod "default-sa-automount" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/explicit-default-sa
  Container:   app
  Message:     Container "app" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/explicit-default-sa
  Container:   app
  Message:     Container "app" image is not pinned by digest (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/explicit-default-sa
  Container:   app
  Message:     Container "app" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

## How to Fix

```yaml

    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
