Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/host-network-pod
  Container:   network-container
  Message:     Container "network-container" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/host-network-pod
  Container:   network-container
  Message:     Container "network-container" image is not pinned by digest (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/host-network-pod
  Container:   network-container
  Message:     Container "network-container" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/host-network-pod
  Container:   network-container
  Message:     Container "network-container" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/host-network-pod
  Message:     Pod "host-network-pod" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/host-network-pod
  Message:     Pod "host-network-pod" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/hostpath-docker-sock
  Container:   docker-sock-mount
  Message:     Container "docker-sock-mount" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/hostpath-docker-sock
  Message:     Pod "hostpath-docker-sock" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/hostpath-docker-sock
  Message:     Pod "hostpath-docker-sock" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/hostpath-docker-sock
  Message:     Pod "hostpath-docker-sock" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/hostpath-etc
  Container:   etc-mount
  Message:     Container "etc-mount" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/hostpath-etc
  Container:   etc-mount
  Message:     Container "etc-mount" image is not pinned by digest (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/hostpath-root
  Message:     Pod "hostpath-root" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/hostpath-var-log
  Container:   log-mount
  Message:     Container "log-mount" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/hostpath-var-log
  Container:   log-mount
  Message:     Container "log-mount" image is not pinned by digest (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/hostpath-var-log
  Container:   log-mount
  Message:     Container "log-mount" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/hostpath-var-log
  Container:   log-mount
  Message:     Container "log-mount" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/hostpath-var-log
  Message:     Pod "hostpath-var-log" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

## How to Fix

```yaml
value: 100000

# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName

[Low] limit-range-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Namespace/kv-e2e-workload
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-workload" has no LimitRange defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a LimitRange, any container can be created without resource constraints. A single runaway or malicious pod can consume all node CPU and memory, causing denial of service for other workloads on the same node.

## How to Fix

Create a LimitRange in the namespace to set default and maximum resource constraints:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 256Mi
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      max:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 1Gi
```

Containers that omit resource requests/limits will inherit these defaults automatically.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.1 recommends LimitRanges for resource governance. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/limit-range/ for configuration details.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] resource-quota-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Namespace/kv-e2e-workload
  Message:     Namespace "kv-e2e-workload" has no ResourceQuota defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a ResourceQuota, a single namespace can consume the entire cluster's CPU, memory, and storage. This creates a noisy-neighbor problem where one team's workloads starve others, and makes capacity planning impossible.

## How to Fix

Create a ResourceQuota to cap the namespace's total resource consumption:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-quota
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "10"
    requests.memory: 20Gi
    limits.cpu: "20"
    limits.memory: 40Gi
    pods: "50"
    services: "10"
```

Tune quota values based on the namespace's actual workload requirements and cluster capacity.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.2 recommends ResourceQuotas for multi-tenant clusters. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/ for quota configuration and enforcement behavior.

[Low] lifecycle-hooks
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/lifecycle-curl
  Container:   curl-hook
  Message:     Container "curl-hook" has a preStop hook with potential network call: "/bin/sh -c curl -s http://monitoring.internal/api/shutdown".
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

PreStop hooks that make network calls (curl, wget, HTTP requests) can be exploited for data exfiltration during pod termination. An attacker who modifies a deployment can add a preStop hook that sends sensitive data to an external server every time a pod is terminated, scaled down, or restarted.

## How to Fix

Replace network-calling preStop hooks with local-only cleanup operations:

```yaml
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    exec:
      command:
        - /bin/sh
        - -c
        - "kill -SIGTERM 1 && sleep 5"  # Graceful local shutdown
```

If external notification is truly required, use a sidecar or controller pattern with egress network policies restricting the destination.

## Learn More

See MITRE ATT&CK T1020 (Automated Exfiltration) for data exfiltration techniques. Network policies should restrict egress for pods that do not need external access.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/lifecycle-httpget
  Message:     Pod "lifecycle-httpget" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/lifecycle-httpget
  Message:     Pod "lifecycle-httpget" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/low-uid-pod
  Container:   low-uid-container
  Message:     Container "low-uid-container" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/low-uid-pod
  Container:   low-uid-container
  Message:     Container "low-uid-container" image is not pinned by digest (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/low-uid-pod
  Container:   low-uid-container
  Message:     Container "low-uid-container" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/low-uid-pod
  Container:   low-uid-container
  Message:     Container "low-uid-container" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/low-uid-pod
  Message:     Pod "low-uid-pod" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] run-as-high-uid
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/low-uid-pod
  Container:   low-uid-container
  Message:     Container "low-uid-container" runs as UID 1000, which is below the recommended minimum of 10000.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

UIDs below 10000 overlap with well-known system accounts on most Linux distributions (e.g., daemon, www-data, nobody). If a container running with a low UID escapes to the host, it may inherit the permissions of that system account, gaining unintended access to host files, sockets, or services owned by that UID.

## How to Fix

Use a high UID that does not overlap with host system accounts:

```yaml
securityContext:
  runAsUser: 65534       # nobody, or any UID >= 10000
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsGroup: 65534
```

Choose a UID >= 10000. The conventional `nobody` UID (65534) is a safe default. Also set the UID in your Dockerfile with `USER 65534` for defense in depth.

## Learn More

This is a defense-in-depth measure. While container UID mapping varies by runtime, using high UIDs avoids accidental privilege overlap on hosts that lack user namespace remapping.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].securityContext.runAsUser
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.2.7 · MITRE T1068 · NSA 1.1

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[1].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/missing-profiles
  Container:   seccomp-only
  Message:     Container "seccomp-only" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[1].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/missing-profiles
  Message:     Deployment "missing-profiles" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/missing-profiles
  Message:     Pod "missing-profiles" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/missing-profiles
  Message:     Deployment "missing-profiles" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/no-startup-probe
  Container:   slow-app
  Message:     Container "slow-app" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/no-startup-probe
  Container:   slow-app
  Message:     Container "slow-app" image is not pinned by digest (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/pull-policy-issues
  Container:   mutable-tag-default
  Message:     Container "mutable-tag-default" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/pull-policy-issues
  Container:   mutable-tag-default
  Message:     Container "mutable-tag-default" image is not pinned by digest (image: nginx:1.25-alpine), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/pull-policy-issues
  Container:   mutable-tag-default
  Message:     Container "mutable-tag-default" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/pull-policy-issues
  Container:   mutable-tag-default
  Message:     Container "mutable-tag-default" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/pull-policy-issues
  Message:     Deployment "pull-policy-issues" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/pull-policy-issues
  Message:     Pod "pull-policy-issues" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/pull-policy-issues
  Message:     Deployment "pull-policy-issues" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/resource-issues
  Container:   no-resources
  Message:     Container "no-resources" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/resource-issues
  Message:     Deployment "resource-issues" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] resource-limits-ratio
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/resource-issues
  Container:   extreme-ratio
  Message:     Container "extreme-ratio" has high limits-to-requests ratio for CPU (10.0x) and memory (16.0x), threshold is 3.0x.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

When resource limits are much higher than requests, the scheduler allocates nodes based on the smaller request values but containers can burst up to their limits. If multiple containers burst simultaneously, the node becomes overcommitted, leading to CPU throttling and OOM kills that cause unpredictable application failures.

## How to Fix

Bring limits closer to requests, ideally within a 3x ratio:

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 200m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 500m            # 2.5x ratio
    memory: 512Mi        # 2x ratio
```

Profile your application's actual resource usage under realistic load using `kubectl top` or Prometheus metrics, then set requests close to the steady-state and limits for peak bursts.

## Learn More

Consider using Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) to automatically recommend appropriate request and limit values. Setting requests equal to limits gives the pod Guaranteed QoS, providing the most predictable performance.
  Field:       .spec.containers[2].resources
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/resource-issues
  Message:     Pod "resource-issues" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] topology-spread
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/resource-issues
  Message:     Deployment "resource-issues" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/unmasked-proc
  Container:   unmasked-proc-container
  Message:     Container "unmasked-proc-container" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/unmasked-proc
  Container:   unmasked-proc-container
  Message:     Container "unmasked-proc-container" image is not pinned by digest (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

  Message:     Pod "unsafe-sysctls-shared-pid" has no topology spread constraints; all replicas may be scheduled on the same node.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without topology spread constraints, the scheduler may place all replicas on the same node or in the same availability zone. If that node or zone fails, your entire service goes down despite having multiple replicas. This negates the high-availability benefits of running multiple pods.

## How to Fix

Add topology spread constraints to distribute replicas across failure domains:

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: my-app
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
```

Use `kubernetes.io/hostname` for node-level spreading and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` for zone-level spreading.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes Pod Topology Spread Constraints documentation. Combining hostname and zone constraints provides both node-level and zone-level fault tolerance.
  Field:       .spec.topologySpreadConstraints
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] ephemeral-storage-limits
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/writable-rootfs
  Container:   no-readonly
  Message:     Container "no-readonly" is missing ephemeral-storage limits.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Ephemeral storage includes container logs, emptyDir volumes, and the writable container layer. Without limits, a single container can fill the node's root disk, triggering eviction of all pods on that node and potentially causing a cascading failure across your cluster. This is a common denial-of-service vector.

## How to Fix

Set ephemeral-storage limits alongside your CPU and memory limits:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
  requests:
    ephemeral-storage: 500Mi
```

Estimate your application's disk usage from logs, temporary files, and cache data. If your application writes large temporary files, consider using a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of ephemeral storage.

## Learn More

The kubelet evicts pods that exceed their ephemeral-storage limit. Use LimitRange to set default ephemeral-storage limits at the namespace level to catch containers that omit this setting.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].resources.limits.ephemeral-storage
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] image-no-digest
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/writable-rootfs
  Container:   no-readonly
  Message:     Container "no-readonly" image is not pinned by digest (image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9), allowing tag mutation.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Image tags are mutable pointers -- a registry administrator or attacker can re-push a different image under the same tag. Without a digest, you have no cryptographic guarantee that the image you deploy is the one you tested.

## How to Fix

Pin images by their SHA-256 content digest for a fully immutable reference:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx@sha256:a8281ce420348a01ea6e   # Immutable
```

Use `crane digest nginx:1.25.3` or `skopeo inspect` to resolve a tag to its digest during CI/CD, then commit the pinned reference.

## Learn More

SLSA Level 1+ and NIST SP 800-190 recommend digest pinning for container supply chain integrity. See the Kubernetes images documentation for details.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].image
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.5.1 · MITRE T1525 · NSA 1.4

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/writable-rootfs
  Container:   no-readonly
  Message:     Container "no-readonly" has no liveness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a liveness probe, Kubernetes cannot detect when a container has become unresponsive or deadlocked. The container continues running and consuming resources while failing to serve traffic. Users experience timeouts and errors until someone manually intervenes.

## How to Fix

Add a liveness probe that checks the container's health:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

Use `httpGet` for HTTP services, `tcpSocket` for TCP services, or `exec` with a custom health check script for non-network workloads.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Set initialDelaySeconds high enough for your application to start, and consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting containers.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].livenessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] liveness-readiness-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/writable-rootfs
  Container:   no-readonly
  Message:     Container "no-readonly" has no readiness probe configured.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes adds the pod to Service endpoints immediately, routing live traffic to containers that may still be initializing or temporarily unable to serve requests. This causes user-facing errors, increased latency, and failed requests during deployments and restarts.

## How to Fix

Add a readiness probe that validates the container can serve traffic:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

The readiness endpoint should check downstream dependencies (database, cache) to confirm the container is truly ready.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes documentation on container probes. Readiness probes control Service endpoint membership, so failing probes remove the pod from load balancing without restarting it.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].readinessProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] priority-class-missing
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/writable-rootfs
  Message:     Deployment "writable-rootfs" has no PriorityClass set; it will be evicted first during resource pressure.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a PriorityClass, pods receive default priority (typically 0) and are among the first to be evicted during resource pressure or node maintenance. This means important application workloads may be killed before less critical ones, leading to unpredictable outages.

## How to Fix

Define PriorityClasses for your workloads and assign them appropriately:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: app-medium
value: 100000
---
# Reference in your workload:
spec:
  priorityClassName: app-medium
```

Create a tiered priority scheme (e.g., app-critical: 500000, app-medium: 100000, app-low: 10000) that reflects your workload importance hierarchy.

## Learn More

Refer to the Kubernetes Pod Priority and Preemption documentation. Establishing a consistent priority scheme across namespaces ensures predictable eviction behavior during resource contention.
  Field:       .spec.priorityClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] runtime-class
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Deployment/writable-rootfs
  Message:     Pod "writable-rootfs" does not specify a RuntimeClass, using the default (unsandboxed) runtime.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a RuntimeClass, pods use the default container runtime (typically runc), which shares the host kernel directly with containers. A kernel vulnerability can allow container escape to the host. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add an additional isolation layer that intercepts system calls or runs containers in lightweight VMs.

## How to Fix

Specify a sandboxed RuntimeClass in the pod spec:

```yaml
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
```

Available RuntimeClasses depend on your cluster configuration. Common options include `gvisor` (user-space kernel), `kata` (micro-VMs), and `firecracker`. Check your cluster's available RuntimeClasses with `kubectl get runtimeclasses`.

## Learn More

Sandboxed runtimes are especially important for multi-tenant clusters and workloads processing untrusted input. They add latency overhead, so evaluate performance requirements. See the Kubernetes RuntimeClass documentation.
  Field:       .spec.runtimeClassName
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1611 · NSA 2.1

[Low] limit-range-missing
  Resource:    local-path-storage/Namespace/local-path-storage
  Message:     Namespace "local-path-storage" has no LimitRange defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a LimitRange, any container can be created without resource constraints. A single runaway or malicious pod can consume all node CPU and memory, causing denial of service for other workloads on the same node.

## How to Fix

Create a LimitRange in the namespace to set default and maximum resource constraints:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 256Mi
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      max:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 1Gi
```

Containers that omit resource requests/limits will inherit these defaults automatically.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.1 recommends LimitRanges for resource governance. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/limit-range/ for configuration details.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Low] resource-quota-missing
  Resource:    local-path-storage/Namespace/local-path-storage
  Message:     Namespace "local-path-storage" has no ResourceQuota defined.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Without a ResourceQuota, a single namespace can consume the entire cluster's CPU, memory, and storage. This creates a noisy-neighbor problem where one team's workloads starve others, and makes capacity planning impossible.

## How to Fix

Create a ResourceQuota to cap the namespace's total resource consumption:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-quota
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "10"
    requests.memory: 20Gi
    limits.cpu: "20"
    limits.memory: 40Gi
    pods: "50"
    services: "10"
```

Tune quota values based on the namespace's actual workload requirements and cluster capacity.

## Learn More

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.2.2 recommends ResourceQuotas for multi-tenant clusters. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/ for quota configuration and enforcement behavior.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5

[Info] rbac-unused-roles
  Resource:    ClusterRole/admin
  Message:     ClusterRole "admin" has no bindings and may be unused.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

Unused Roles and ClusterRoles are dormant permissions waiting to be activated. An attacker who can create or modify RoleBindings could bind these unused roles to gain additional privileges. They also create confusion during audits and make it harder to understand the actual RBAC posture.

## How to Fix

Verify the role is truly unused, then remove it:

```bash
# Check for any bindings referencing this role
kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A \
  -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.roleRef.name=="unused-role")'

# Remove the unused role
kubectl delete clusterrole unused-role
kubectl delete role unused-role -n my-namespace
```

Implement a regular RBAC hygiene process to review and clean up unused roles quarterly.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes RBAC best practices documentation and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark section 5.1 for guidance on maintaining a clean RBAC configuration.
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.1.1 · MITRE T1078 · NSA 3.1

[Info] startup-probes
  Resource:    kv-e2e-workload/Pod/no-startup-probe
  Container:   slow-app
  Message:     Container "slow-app" has a liveness probe but no startup probe, which can cause restart loops during slow startup.
  Remediation: ## Why This Matters

When a container has a liveness probe but no startup probe, the liveness probe starts checking immediately after the container starts. If the application takes longer to initialize than the liveness probe's initialDelaySeconds + failureThreshold allows, Kubernetes kills and restarts the container, creating an infinite restart loop (CrashLoopBackOff).

## How to Fix

Add a startup probe that gives the container enough time to initialize:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    startupProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      failureThreshold: 30     # 30 x 10s = 5 minutes to start
      periodSeconds: 10
```

The liveness probe is disabled until the startup probe succeeds, giving slow-starting applications the time they need.

## Learn More

See the Kubernetes startup probe documentation. This is especially important for Java/JVM applications, containers loading large ML models, or services that run database migrations on startup.
  Field:       .spec.containers[0].startupProbe
  Frameworks:  CIS 5.6.3 · MITRE T1499 · NSA 1.5
